After that, any hint of heat or raised voices could send Marta straight into the habits that felt safest to her: she would leave a room, end a conversation, or throw herself into work so she would not have to sit with the surge of fear. Every time she later heard raised voices or saw fire in an ordinary setting, the scene did not just frighten her; it immediately turned into self-judgment, as if the cue itself carried the verdict that she had failed to protect anyone and was not the kind of person who could stay calm when it mattered. Flames rose unexpectedly at the roadside, people shouted, and for a few terrible minutes Marta was close enough to hear the panic in voices and the crackle of burning. She had not been the one directly in danger, but she had watched others caught in it, and afterward she kept returning to the same thought: she should have protected them and failed. That belief settled quickly into a harsher comparison, that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, and from there she began to regard the event as proof that she was somehow less capable than she had assumed. The more she told herself that she should have handled it differently, the more the memory seemed to come back on its own, fixed in place as proof of her failure, and she found herself pulled back into the scene over and over until it felt more vivid than an ordinary recollection. Each time the flashback came, she was left thinking that she had let it happen and that it said something permanent about who she was. Even now, when she tried to explain what the memory felt like, she would say it was more real and vivid than ordinary recollections, as if it had not happened in the past at all but remained stored somewhere sharp and immediate. Each time that image broke through again, it left her thinking that if it could still happen to her so vividly, there must be something permanently wrong with her, and that thought settled into the same harsh belief that she was weak and should have done better. Those appraisals did not stay separate from the memory; they fed it, pulling her back to the roadside scene and making it harder to see as something finished. The more she judged herself for failing, the more the image sharpened and returned, as if the memory had latched onto those criticisms and used them to force itself back into view. The more she told herself she had failed, the more the image of the fire and the panic seemed to return on its own, proof of the same failure. The sound of shouting and the crackle of flames could come back inside her head when she thought about it, and the memory often arrived without warning, triggered by something small and ordinary. After it hit, she reached for whatever would shut the images down: she threw herself into work, stayed late at the office in Boston, and filled weekends with chores so there would be no quiet moment for the scene to take hold. Once those reminders hit, Marta would start changing what she did almost immediately: she avoided the places and situations that carried the same feel, kept herself busy, and made decisions designed to stop the alarm from rising again. Once the memory broke through, the danger did not feel like something that had happened in the past; it felt immediate and physical, as if the fire and panic had simply moved back into her body. The memory left her scanning for those cues almost before she knew she was doing it, as though the scene had taught her body to treat them all as warnings. Even in her own kitchen, with the doors locked, she could feel herself scanning for what might go wrong next. The strategies that were supposed to protect her had, in effect, kept the alarm alive. Marta’s negative appraisals deepened as this cycle went on. Each return of the images seemed to confirm that she had failed to protect others, that she was the sort of person who froze when it mattered most, and that someone else would have handled it better. The more vividly she replayed the event, the more she judged herself against that imagined stronger person, and the harsher those judgments became. She began to wonder whether her life was worth living anymore, not in a dramatic or impulsive way but as a bleak conclusion reached after months of feeling trapped inside the same scene. By the time she came for help, she was exhausted from trying to outrun the memories and frightened by how quickly the world could still change shape around her.
